chapter: Moving, Columbia Missouri and leaving home
title: Fats Waller's unhappiness and jazz as offsetting madness with happiness
summary: Thompson says black people covered fear with humor and drink, and that real jazz and blues expressed the ability to offset madness with happiness.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I had heard about it, I heard people talk about it, you know in fact many people, many black people

joke about it. In fact a lot of people wonder how do black people joke about these things that have passed, you know, and how they make it, you know. They look like they're having a good time all the time, which is not really necessarily true, like I told you about Fats Waller Fats Wallick.
Yes.
I don't think Fats Waller Fats Wallick was happy. Any human being who is intelligent enough to be able to produce art is ignorant enough to be happy with as the circumstances that is unpleasant.
That's right.
But they use alcohol or what not, or just gesture to overcome this to keep from being violent.
Right.
You see. The fact of the matter is I think people should be very, very appreciative and grateful that the masses of black people were really good people.
Yes, they were.

Because of the fact that they took whiskey and other things, parties, like the parties I played in. It was through the parties I played that people were able to give vent to their fears, and instead of fighting back, they just waited and bided their time until they could do something else --
Found what happiness they could.
That's right. And that's what -- that was possible
(Inaudible) to them.

Right. Which is a combination of what my music is about, what any true jazz is doing when they play music. And it's one of the reasons why I said, as we perhaps discuss before I finish why the jazz that's being played today that's categorized as jazz is not really real true jazz. You know?
I think it's a very interesting point.
Because they're not saying musically what jazz originally started out to say.
Yes.
Which is an expression, musically, of mainly this ability to offset madness with happiness.
Very good.
And there might be an interpretation of the real blues.
Very [Good] very well-done, yes. [PAUSE]
